finalResponse:
# Fourth Pass — The Snack Line

*Same house style. And the same structural gap as last time: the brief says "a target international market" without naming one. I've stopped waiting to be told and picked one, on stated grounds, and built the thing so that most of it survives being told I picked wrong. Substitution notes are at the end.*

---

## The thing that is not being said in the research

"Consumers want new and interesting snack options" is what consumers say in every market, in every study, including the ones where launch after launch dies at week fourteen. Novelty is a *trial* driver. It has almost no relationship to the thing we actually sell, which is the fourth purchase.

So I'd read that finding as a sentence about **awareness cost**, not about product. It says: we can get tried. It says nothing about whether we can get bought again. The commercial question — the one the deck doesn't ask — is what the repeat rate is at twelve weeks against local incumbents who have been iterating on the same three flavours for twenty years and can make a pack for less than our packaging costs.

I'd also note quietly that "distinct local tastes" is being framed as a flavour problem. It isn't. Flavour is the cheapest thing to fix and the easiest to buy in. The hard constraints are format, price per pack, ambient temperature and who owns the shelf. Those decide the product. Flavour merely decorates it.

## Which market, and why this one

**Indonesia.** Two hundred and eighty million people, a snacking habit that isn't a habit so much as a continuous background activity (*ngemil* runs all day and doesn't compete with meals), the youngest median age of any large market we could reach, and — the part I find most interesting — a category where the dominant local players are excellent at price and poor at consistency. That gap is a place a foreign manufacturer can stand.

It is also, deliberately, a market where several of our comfortable assumptions break: most volume moves through hundreds of thousands of small independent outlets rather than modern trade, there is effectively no cold chain outside the cities, halal certification is a licence to trade rather than a claim on the pack, and the meaningful price ceiling is a single coin, not a margin percentage. If we can build here, the discipline travels. If we build for Singapore or Seoul first, it doesn't.

## The constraints, before any idea

Written down first because every idea below is downstream of them.

- **Price per pack, not price per kilo.** There is a sachet tier at roughly two to three thousand rupiah that is the entry price for a daily purchase. If our cost structure can't reach it, we are a premium brand whether we intended to be one or not — and premium is a real strategy, but let's choose it rather than discover it.
- **Thirty-two degrees and eighty per cent humidity, for weeks, on a shelf with no air conditioning, having arrived by motorbike.** Crunch retention and oil stability are not quality-assurance details here. They are the product. They are also, usefully, a genuine technical moat: it is the thing our process engineering can do that a regional *keripik* maker cannot.
- **Halal, properly.** Not the logo — the whole chain. Flavour carriers, alcohol-based extracts, enzymes, emulsifiers, shared lines at the co-packer. Get this wrong once and there is no recovery, only exit. The regulatory deadlines have already moved once and may move again; that is not a reason to be relaxed, it's a reason to be early.
- **Texture vocabulary is the language of preference.** *Kriuk*, *kriuk-kriuk*, *gurih*. Preference is described texturally before it is described by taste. Our development panel should be sorting on mouthfeel first. That will feel wrong to a flavour-led marketing team.
- **Foreignness cuts both ways.** It buys hygiene, consistency and a certain aspirational gloss. It cannot buy authenticity in a *rujak* flavour. So: borrow authenticity, don't invent it.

## The line, in two halves that do different jobs

I'd split the portfolio explicitly, because a portfolio that tries to be both novel and dependable is neither.

**The core — three SKUs, built for repeat, changed reluctantly.**

**1. The meal companion.** A high-crunch savoury crisp positioned to be eaten *with* rice, not instead of a meal — the *kerupuk* adjacency. Sambal-forward, *gurih*, engineered so it survives being opened, half-eaten and left on a table for three hours in that humidity. This is the strategically valuable idea in the whole document, because it moves us out of the snack budget and into the meal budget, where purchase is daily and doesn't require an occasion. Resealable, mid-size, family-priced.

**2. The sachet.** Single-serve extruded corn or tapioca puff, sweet-savoury-hot, at the coin price, sold on the hanging strip at the front of a *warung*. Thin margin bordering on none. I'd defend it anyway: it is not a profit centre, it is a billboard that pays for its own printing and buys us the physical shelf position from which everything else is sold. Judge it on outlets reached, not contribution.

**3. The evening sharing bag.** Larger, louder, built for watching something together. Two flavours in one dual-compartment bag, because sharing implies disagreement and nobody has priced that in.

**The rotation — where "new and interesting" is allowed to live.**

**4. Limited local collaborations,** two or three a year. A regionally famous sambal maker, a cult *keripik* brand, a specific city's street preparation. Small runs, deliberately scarce, engineered for social sharing. This is how we feed the appetite for novelty without betting the core on it — and it lets us buy authenticity by the batch rather than pretending to it.

**5. Sour, not sweet.** The *rujak* / *asinan* logic — young mango, tamarind, chilli-salt: sour, hot, sweet and salty at once. This is the flavour space furthest from anything in our current book and the one I'd be least willing to develop in a home lab. Partner locally or don't do it.

**6. Satiety, framed as value, never as health.** Baked, legume-based — tempeh, soy, edamame — aimed at students and young urban workers who are skipping meals for reasons of money and time. The word is "filling," not "healthy." Healthy framed as sacrifice fails in price-sensitive markets; framed as *more meal for the same coin* it doesn't.

**7. The seasonal tin.** Ramadan and Lebaran gifting sits adjacent to *kue kering* and represents a margin peak that can fund the rest of the year. Reusable tin, gift architecture, our formats in familiar festive flavour codes. Co-pack it entirely — I don't want to own a line that runs eight weeks a year.

## How I'd get it into the market

Co-packing before capital. Rent someone else's extruder, badly, for eighteen months rather than buying our own well. Modular over fixed steel — the same argument I made about warehouse robots and for the same reason: we will be wrong about something, and we should be wrong in an asset we can walk away from.

One city, one distributor, one traditional-trade cluster deliberately run differently from the modern-trade launch, so we can see which mechanic actually worked rather than reading a blended national average that conceals both. And I'd stage the distributor agreement rather than signing the national one that will be offered: sell-in targets are hit with enthusiasm and tell you nothing. Everything I want to know appears at reorder.

## How we'd know

Repeat rate at twelve weeks, by SKU. Rate of sale per outlet per week — not shipments. Weighted distribution alongside out-of-stock rate, because the second number is what tells you whether the first one is real. Gross margin per pack *after* trade spend and breakage. Texture-complaint rate by month, which is our humidity early-warning system. And returns as a proportion of dispatch, by route.

One metric I'd refuse: brand awareness. It will look excellent, it will be purchased, and it will be cited at exactly the moment the reorder numbers are inconvenient.

## What I'd resist

Focus groups asked whether they'd like something new. A flavour named in the head office and translated afterwards. National listing in year one. A celebrity face bought before the repeat rate exists. Any SKU whose business case depends on modern trade alone. And the "authentic local flavour, made properly at last" positioning, which reads as condescension in every market it has ever been tried in.

---

If the named market turns out to be Vietnam, the Philippines or Mexico, most of this stands: the two-half portfolio, the meal-companion insight, the coin-priced sachet as distribution purchase, co-pack before capital, repeat rate over awareness. What changes is the flavour architecture, the halal chain becomes a different compliance problem, and the seasonal peak moves. If it turns out to be Japan or Korea, almost none of it stands and I'd want to start again, because in those markets the constraint is retailer power and shelf rotation speed, not price and heat.

The pattern, once: this isn't a flavour brief. It's a distribution decision wearing a flavour brief's clothes, with a novelty programme bolted on the side to satisfy a research finding that was never really about product.

Two things I'd want and don't have: whether we intend to own manufacturing in-market eventually, and our actual cost-of-goods ceiling. The first decides whether the co-pack is a bridge or a permanent arrangement. The second decides whether the sachet tier exists at all — and without it, this is a different, smaller, more comfortable plan.

I'll proceed as though the answers are the ones I'd least like.
